issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court must address the material factual and legal questions raised by the record when deciding an appeal, and a judgment that fails to do so may be set aside and remitted for a fresh decision.
material_facts: The High Court was deciding an appeal from a trial court decree in a suit seeking a declaration of ownership and other reliefs based in part on adverse possession.

The High Court's judgment did not resolve material questions, including whether the earlier judgment bound the defendants, whether a tenant's possession could count toward the claimant's period of possession, and the effect of earlier findings concerning ownership and possession.
The Supreme Court found serious errors in the High Court's judgment but expressly declined to decide the merits of the title or adverse-possession claims.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the High Court's judgment was set aside, and the matter was remitted to the High Court for a fresh decision of the first appeal in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal under Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the first appellate court must determine the material questions arising from the case and evaluate the facts relevant to them. Whether possession amounts to ouster or adverse possession is a legal conclusion or a mixed question of law and fact to be drawn from proved facts. The Supreme Court exercised its jurisdiction under Article 136 to set aside the materially deficient judgment and order a de novo decision. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.first_appeal_from_trial_decree: A party appealed from a trial court decree to a court exercising first-appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.material_legal_questions_unresolved: The first appellate court left material factual or legal questions raised by the case unresolved.

issues.definition: When a first appeal from a trial decree leaves material questions unresolved, the first appellate judgment is set aside and the matter is returned for a fresh decision.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant relying on adverse possession must plead and prove the facts establishing actual, hostile, continuous, exclusive, and undisturbed possession to the knowledge of the true owner.
material_facts: The claimant sought ownership on the basis of alleged possession extending over time.

The Supreme Court stated that the claim required pleading and proof of actual possession, the period and date from which possession was claimed, continuity, exclusivity, lack of disturbance, and a hostile claim communicated to the true owner.
The Supreme Court did not decide whether those requirements were satisfied on the evidence and expressly left the merits for the High Court on remand.
issues.conclusion: A claim to ownership by adverse possession requires the claimant to plead and prove the specified elements; the Supreme Court made no determination that the claimant in this case had done so.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides for extinguishment of the lawful owner's right to property when the owner does not sue for possession within the time allowed by law. A claimant relying on adverse possession must plead and prove the date and period of actual possession, that it was continuous, exclusive and undisturbed to the knowledge of the true owner, and that the claimant asserted and communicated a hostile title. The Court identified the application of Article 64, including whether a tenant's possession could be counted as the claimant's possession, as a question left for determination on remand.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: The claimant asserted a right to property on the basis of adverse possession.
predicates.claimant_seeks_ownership_by_prescriptive: The claimant relied on possession over time as the basis for claiming ownership.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks ownership through adverse possession, the claimant must plead and prove possession that is hostile, continuous, exclusive, and undisturbed.
